review.requirement_proposition: AI actors should provide meaningful information making stakeholders aware of interactions with AI, including workplace interactions.

previous_canonical_assessment.applicability_basis: OECD Section 1.3(ii) is used as a nonbinding comparative benchmark for AI actors and affected workplace/identity-decision stakeholders in the February 2025 Pindrop interview, not as proof of adoption or a legal duty. Synthetic applicant representation and detection materially engage workplace awareness; adverse screening/identity decisions engage affected-person challenge information.
previous_canonical_assessment.finding_basis: The sources for the February 2025 Pindrop interview establish the occurrence and detection/account-opening sequence, but do not preserve the responsible actor’s complete interaction disclosures, affected-person notices or information enabling challenges. Detection alone is not provision of that information. Neither adequate provision nor its absence is independently proved; the benchmark finding is evidence-insufficient.

review.reason_for_change: Pindrop reports that the applicant presented a synthetic visual identity as an ordinary person during a paid-role interview; the employer discovered the face swap through its own detector, with no reported applicant disclosure of the AI-mediated representation. The initial presentation therefore failed the workplace-interaction awareness benchmark in this bounded first-party account. Later detection supplied awareness but did not make the earlier deceptive presentation transparent. The result does not assert a hire, liability or generator-wide controls.

conclusion_change.previous: The human-directed applicant used an AI-mediated false visual presentation to seek a paid engineering role. The attempted employment decision had a materially misleading identity premise even though Pindrop detected the face swap during interview and reports no hire. Detection identifies the false presentation, but continuation to a coding assessment leaves containment and the adequacy of the downstream response unresolved; it does not erase the attempted deceptive economic solicitation. The record does not attribute the applicant’s objective or tactic selection to the AI system, or infer a generator-side consent failure. Attempted AI-mediated employment solicitation is established, but detection and later coding-stage continuation do not prove containment. OECD transparency and contestability are nonbinding comparative benchmarks; the available detector report does not establish the responsible actor’s disclosures or affected-person challenge information. Other voluntary frameworks remain adoption- and object-bounded, without a conformance finding.
